sessions.lesson:
A real sequence assigns a real number a_n to each integer n≥1. A tail starts at an index N and includes every n≥N. “Eventually P(n)” means there is one N after which P holds for every index. “Infinitely often P(n)” means that after any proposed cutoff there is another success; failures may continue too. “For all n” also controls the finite beginning.
Worked example: a_n=1/n. The assertion a_n<1/5 is false at n=5 but holds for every n≥6, so it is eventual. For b_n=(-1)^n, b_n=1 holds at all even indices and fails at every odd one: infinitely often, but not eventually. The formula, not a graph of a few terms, justifies these conclusions.
Guided practice: For c_n=2 when n≤4 and c_n=0 afterwards, is c_n=0 always or eventually true? Choose a cutoff, then ask whether a larger cutoff also works. Check: eventually, N=5 and every larger N work; n=1 refutes “always”. A tail can ignore finitely many exceptions; it cannot ignore a recurring kind of exception.

sessions.lesson:
The distance |a_n-L| is the error relative to a proposed limit L. We write a_n→L when for every ε>0 there exists an integer N≥1 such that every n≥N satisfies |a_n-L|<ε. Read in order: a challenger chooses ε; you choose N using ε; the challenger may then choose any n≥N. You cannot adjust N to that last n. Infinity is not a final index.
Worked example: a_n=3+2/n tends to 3. Its error is 2/n. For any ε>0 choose N=floor(2/ε)+1, where floor(t) is the greatest integer ≤t. Then N>2/ε, so n≥N gives 2/n≤2/N<ε. This is a proof for every accuracy, not just decimal evidence. Any larger integer N also works.
Guided practice: For a_n=-1+1/(n+2), write its error, then choose a sufficient N. Check: error 1/(n+2); N=floor(1/ε)+1 is conservative and valid. Explain the chain n+2>N>1/ε rather than merely naming N.

sessions.lesson:
An error budget is a requested inequality, not a rounded decimal. A sufficient cutoff proves a guarantee; the least cutoff additionally proves failure just before it when that index exists. If the exact error is C/n with C>0, strict error<ε means n>C/ε. The least integer satisfying this is floor(C/ε)+1. For error≤ε, equality may be allowed instead.
Worked example: error 4/n<0.2 requires n>20, hence N=21. N=20 fails because its error is exactly0.2. If the specification changes to ≤0.2, N=20 works. Units must agree: an error in metres must be compared with a tolerance in metres.
Guided practice: error2/(n+1)<0.3 requires n>17/3. Check N=6 and its predecessor n=5: 2/7<0.3 but 2/6>0.3. The expression may decrease with n; establish that monotonicity from positive denominators before concluding the entire tail is safe.

sessions.lesson:
Negate the definition one quantifier at a time. Failure of a_n→L means: there exists ε₀>0 such that for every N there exists n≥N with |a_n-L|≥ε₀. The tolerance is fixed; the bad index may depend on N. One early failure proves nothing about the tail. Also, refuting one proposed L does not yet refute every possible finite limit.
Worked example: a_n=0 on even n and 2 on odd n does not tend to0. Choose ε₀=1; for any N choose an odd n≥N. Then error2≥1. To rule out every L directly, note |L|+|2-L|≥2 (distance along the line cannot be shorter than the endpoint distance). At least one of these two errors is ≥1 and recurs arbitrarily late.
Guided practice: A sequence equals5 at perfect squares and0 elsewhere. Refute limit0. Check ε₀=1 and n=k² with k²≥N. Sparse exceptions still defeat an eventual guarantee.

sessions.lesson:
The triangle inequality says |u+v|≤|u|+|v|: travelling via an intermediate point cannot shorten the direct distance. It follows from -|u|≤u≤|u| and the same inequalities for v, then addition. Thus |A-B|≤|A-a_n|+|a_n-B|.
Worked proof: suppose a_n tends to distinct A and B. Put d=|A-B|>0. For tolerance d/3 there are cutoffs N_A and N_B for the two claims. Choose n≥max(N_A,N_B), so both bounds hold at the same index. Then d<d/3+d/3=2d/3, impossible. Therefore A=B. Choosing the larger cutoff is essential.
Guided practice: If two estimates u and v are each within0.04 of the same number z, bound |u-v|. Check: it is <0.08, not necessarily <0.04. Draw three points on a number line if the error addition is unclear.

sessions.lesson:
A sequence is bounded if some finite B≥0 satisfies |a_n|≤B for every n. If a_n→L, use ε=1 to get a tail with |a_n-L|<1. Triangle inequality gives |a_n|<|L|+1 there. Only a_1,…,a_(N-1) remain; finitely many real numbers have a largest absolute value. Taking the maximum of these and |L|+1 bounds the entire sequence. This proves convergence implies boundedness.
Worked example: let a_1=-80 and a_n=2/n for n≥2. The tail is bounded by1, but B=1 misses the first term; B=80 works globally. The sequence still tends to0, since that first term can be bypassed.
Guided practice: Is (-1)^n bounded? Does it converge? Check: B=1 bounds it, but the recurring values -1 and1 prevent convergence. Boundedness is necessary for a finite limit, not sufficient.

sessions.lesson:
If a_n→A and b_n→B, then a_n+b_n→A+B. Given ε>0, make each error <ε/2 after its own cutoff and take the larger cutoff. Triangle inequality bounds the sum error by their sum, <ε. For c a_n with fixed c≠0, request input error ε/|c|; c=0 is immediate. These arguments also yield subtraction and finite linear combinations.
Worked example: if |a_n-2|≤1/n and |b_n+1|≤3/n, then |(2a_n-b_n)-5|≤2/n+3/n=5/n. Any integer N>5/ε certifies the output error. A negative coefficient contributes its absolute value to an error budget.
Eventual order is preserved weakly: if a_n≤b_n eventually and both converge, A≤B. If A>B, use errors<(A-B)/3 on a common tail; these force a_n>b_n, contradiction. Strict order need not stay strict in the limit: 0<1/n but both sides tend to0.
Guided practice: With errors bounded by2/n and1/n, bound the error of a_n+4b_n. Check: ≤6/n; the guarantees must apply simultaneously.

sessions.lesson:
For a_n→A and b_n→B, rewrite a_nb_n-AB=a_n(b_n-B)+B(a_n-A). Convergence bounds |a_n| by some K≥1. Make |b_n-B|<ε/(2K) and |a_n-A|<ε/(2(|B|+1)) on a shared tail; the product error is <ε. Thus products converge to products of limits.
If B≠0, eventually |b_n-B|<|B|/2. The triangle inequality gives |b_n|≥|B|-|b_n-B|>|B|/2, so b_n is nonzero there. Then |1/b_n-1/B|=|b_n-B|/(|b_n||B|)≤2|b_n-B|/|B|²→0. Combine with the product law for quotients.
Worked example: (2+1/n)/(4-1/n)→1/2; for n≥1 its denominator is≥3. In contrast, numerator and denominator both tending to0 does not specify a quotient limit. The pairs (1/n)/(1/n) and (1/n²)/(1/n) give1 and0.
Guided practice: Bound below 5+(-1)^n/n. Check: ≥4, so reciprocals are safe; its limit is5 because the error is≤1/n.

sessions.lesson:
If l_n≤a_n≤u_n eventually and l_n,u_n→L, then a_n→L. Given ε>0, both outer sequences eventually lie between L-ε and L+ε; a_n must too. Equivalently, if |a_n-L|≤e_n and e_n→0 with e_n≥0, the error envelope proves the limit. An oscillating sign does not prevent its amplitude from shrinking.
Worked example: a_n=2+(-1)^n/(n+1). Its distance from2 equals1/(n+1), which tends to0. It crosses its limit repeatedly but converges. No monotonicity claim about a_n is needed.
Guided practice: If -3/n≤b_n≤4/n for all n, what follows? Check b_n→0; |b_n|≤4/n yields the explicit certificate N>4/ε. The squeeze needs the same limiting value on both sides. Merely -1≤b_n≤1 does not determine a limit.

sessions.lesson:
For q=0, q^n=0 for n≥1; for q=1 it is1. If 0<q<1, write 1/q=1+c with c>0. Bernoulli’s inequality (1+c)^n≥1+nc follows by induction: multiplying the n-case by1+c adds a nonnegative nc² term. Hence 0<q^n≤1/(1+nc)→0. If -1<q<0, apply this to |q| and squeeze |q^n|. For q>1 the same inequality gives unbounded growth past every threshold; q=-1 alternates; q<-1 has alternating signs with growing magnitude.
Worked example: q=3/4 has c=1/3, so (3/4)^n≤1/(1+n/3). Choosing integer N>3/ε makes this <ε. It is conservative, but proves convergence without a logarithm or derivative.
Guided practice: Classify (-1/3)^n and (-3)^n. Check: the first tends to0; the second has no finite limit and does not tend to positive infinity because of its negative odd terms.

sessions.lesson:
A subsequence a_(n_k) selects terms using strictly increasing positive integers n_1<n_2<…. Its new index is k. Induction gives n_k≥k, so the selected indices eventually pass any fixed cutoff. If a_n→L, the original ε-cutoff N also works for k≥N: n_k≥k≥N. Therefore every subsequence has that same limit.
Worked example: a_n=1+(-1)^n has even subsequence2 and odd subsequence0. If the whole sequence converged, both subsequences would share its unique limit. They do not, so it diverges. A single convergent subsequence only describes some selected terms.
Guided practice: If a_n→4, what is lim a_(3k+2)? Check 4; indices3k+2 increase and escape all finite cutoffs. Selecting a_2 repeatedly is not a subsequence under this definition.

sessions.lesson:
Increasing here means nondecreasing: a_(n+1)≥a_n. Decreasing means nonincreasing. An increasing real sequence bounded above converges; a decreasing one bounded below converges. The real-number fact behind this theorem is completeness: every nonempty set of reals bounded above has a least upper bound, called its supremum. We use that fact here, without constructing the real numbers.
Proof for increasing a_n: let L=sup{a_n}. All terms≤L. For any ε>0, L-ε is not an upper bound, so some a_N>L-ε. Monotonicity then puts every n≥N in (L-ε,L], hence |a_n-L|<ε. Negating a decreasing sequence gives the other case.
Worked example: a_n=5-1/n is increasing and bounded above by5 (also by100). The theorem proves convergence; its formula identifies limit5, not100. A bound need not be the least upper bound.
Guided practice: Is increasing alone enough? Check a_n=n: increasing, but it crosses every finite bound. Is boundedness alone enough? Recall the two alternating values in S11.

sessions.lesson:
A recurrence defines the next term from the current one. A set is invariant when starting inside it forces the next term to remain inside; induction then controls every term. A fixed point solves x=F(x), but a trajectory need not approach it. First establish convergence, then justify passing the limit through the recurrence using an applicable law.
Worked example: x_1=1, x_(n+1)=(x_n+4)/2. If1≤x_n≤4, the next term lies between2.5 and4, so [1,4] is invariant. Also x_(n+1)-x_n=(4-x_n)/2≥0. Monotone bounded convergence supplies L. The shifted sequence x_(n+1) has the same limit (it omits one term); sum/scalar laws give L=(L+4)/2, hence L=4.
Guided practice: The rule y_(n+1)=2-y_n has fixed point1. Start y_1=0 and compute four terms. Check 0,2,0,2: the fixed point exists but this trajectory does not converge. Never substitute a hypothetical limit without establishing its existence.

sessions.lesson:
The statement a_n→+∞ means: for every M>0 there is N so that n≥N implies a_n>M. It describes persistent growth, not a real-valued limit. For -∞ require a_n<-M eventually. An unbounded sequence only has arbitrarily large magnitude somewhere; it need not stay beyond a threshold. Do not apply finite-limit arithmetic to infinity as though it were a number.
Worked example: a_n=2n-5 tends to+∞. For M>0 choose integer N>(M+5)/2. All n≥N then satisfy2n-5>M. But b_n=(-1)^n n has unbounded magnitude and no signed infinite limit: positive even terms refute -∞, negative odd terms refute+∞.
Guided practice: For c_n=-n², choose a cutoff forcing c_n<-M. Check any integer N>sqrt(M) works. To rule out a signed infinite limit, exhibit failures arbitrarily far out, not only near the start.

sessions.lesson:
For a real function, inputs approach a finite point a through its domain; they do not march along only integer indices. The statement lim_(x→a) f(x)=L asks for f(x) close toL whenever x is sufficiently close to a but x≠a. A punctured neighborhood is 0<|x-a|<δ. We consider points with domain inputs arbitrarily close; otherwise a limit definition would become vacuous. Two-sided limits here use domains with nearby inputs on both sides unless a relative-domain limit is explicitly stated.
Worked example: f(x)=x+2 for x≠1, but f(1)=90. As x→1 the nearby values tend to3. Changing the single value90 to anything else does not change that limit. A function can even be undefined at1 and have the same limit.
Guided practice: If g(x)=4 for every x≠0 and g(0)=-6, find lim_(x→0)g(x) and g(0). Check 4 and-6. A table or graph suggests nearby behavior; a formula and a neighborhood argument certify it.

sessions.lesson:
The finite function-limit definition is: for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that every domain input x with 0<|x-a|<δ satisfies |f(x)-L|<ε. Epsilon measures output error; delta controls input distance. Delta may depend on ε and the fixed a and formula, but not on the later x. Compared with sequences, an index cutoff N is replaced by a neighborhood radius δ.
Worked example: prove lim_(x→2)(3x+1)=7. Error=3|x-2|. Given ε>0 choose δ=ε/3. If0<|x-2|<δ, error<3δ=ε. For a constant function, error is0 and any positive δ works. For slope m≠0, δ=ε/|m| handles either sign.
Guided practice: For f(x)=-2x+6 as x→1, compute the target and a valid δ. Check L=4 andδ=ε/2. A smaller positive delta also works; there is usually no obligation to find the largest one.

Guided practice: For g(x)=x+4 on x<1 and3x+2 on x>1, check both limits equal5. Any assigned g(1) leaves the limit5; only g(1)=5 makes it continuous, a concept we will formalize later.

sessions.lesson:
Function sum, product and quotient laws parallel sequence laws: synchronize neighborhoods using the smaller delta; bound factors locally for products; keep denominators away from0 for quotients. Thus polynomials have their substituted limits, and rational functions do wherever the denominator’s limit is nonzero.
If f and g agree throughout some punctured neighborhood of a, their limits at a agree even if their domains differ at a. This licenses cancellation of a common factor only where that factor is nonzero.
Worked example: (x²-16)/(x-4)=x+4 when x≠4. Near4, excluding4 itself, the original equals x+4, so its limit is8. The original expression is still undefined at4. Cancellation is multiplication-factor cancellation, not deleting terms in a sum.
Guided practice: Find lim_(x→-2)(x²+5x+6)/(x+2). Factor first. Check(x+2)(x+3)/(x+2)=x+3 off-2, hence limit1, with the hole retained.
For a denominator changing sign near0 while the numerator stays above a positive constant, the quotient has arbitrarily large positive values on one side and negative values on the other. No finite limit can cover those values. S23 will formalize this with threshold neighborhoods.

The notation0/0 describes separate numerator and denominator limits; it is not a number. Seek an identity valid at nearby legal inputs. For radicals, multiply by the conjugate: (√u-√v)(√u+√v)=u-v. Check radicands and avoid multiplying or dividing by zero.

Worked example: (√(x+4)-2)/x becomes1/(√(x+4)+2) for x≠0 near0; limit1/4. The original still has a hole at0.
Guided practice: Rationalize (√(9+h)-3)/h. Check 1/(√(9+h)+3), hence limit1/6 as h→0. The decisive pattern is taught; the assessment must still require choosing legal transformations and interpreting the result.

sessions.lesson:
Angles in this session are radians. For 0<t<π/2 compare areas in the unit circle: the triangle with vertices the origin, (1,0), (cos t,sin t) has area sin t/2; the sector has area t/2 (fraction t/(2π) of disk areaπ); the outer triangle formed by the ray at angle t and the tangent x=1 has area tan t/2. Containment gives sin t≤t≤tan t, hence cos t≤sin t/t≤1.
We still need cos t→1 without assuming it. The unit-circle identity gives 1-cos t=sin²t/(1+cos t). In this neighborhood cos t>0 and |sin t|≤|t|, so 0≤1-cos t≤t²→0. Symmetry sin(-t)=-sin t and cos(-t)=cos t extends the bounds to negative t. Squeeze now proves sin t/t→1.
Worked example: sin(3x)/(2x)=(3/2)[sin(3x)/(3x)]→3/2. The new input3x tends to0. Also x² sin(1/x)→0 because its absolute value≤x²; sin(1/x) itself need not approach a value.
Guided practice: Evaluate sin(4h)/(7h) and justify the substitution. Check 4/7, with t=4h→0. Degrees would introduce a conversion factor; the base theorem is in radians.
A function limit at0 also controls every sequence of nonzero domain inputs tending to0: its delta-neighborhood eventually contains all those inputs. Thus two such input sequences with different output limits refute a function limit. This is a one-way test here; one successful input sequence is insufficient.

Divide polynomial ratios by the highest denominator power and use1/x→0 and its powers. The proof1/x→0 at either end is |1/x|<ε whenever|x|>1/ε. With radicals, √(x²)=|x|: factoring out x² from a square root keeps its absolute-value square root.
Worked example: (4x²+x)/(2x²+7)→2 at either end. Also √(x²+9)/x=(|x|/x)√(1+9/x²), giving1 at+∞ and-1 at-∞.

The statement f(x)→+∞ as x→a means: for every M>0 there exists δ>0 such that every domain input with0<|x-a|<δ has f(x)>M. For -∞ use f(x)<-M. One-sided versions restrict the side. sessions.lesson:
A function is continuous at a domain point a when lim_(x→a)f(x)=f(a). This requires a defined value and a matching nearby limit. At an endpoint of a domain interval we use the appropriate one-sided limit. Polynomials are continuous everywhere; rational functions are continuous where their denominators are nonzero, by the established limit laws. Square roots are continuous on their real domain by S20.
A removable discontinuity has a finite nearby limit that can fill or replace a single value. A jump with different side limits cannot be repaired by changing only the point value.
Worked example: h(x)=(x²-1)/(x-1) off1 has limit2 there; seth(1)=2 for its continuous extension. For f(x)=0 onx<0 and1 onx>0, no choice off(0) can match both sides.
Guided practice: On[0,∞), √x is continuous at0: for 0≤x<ε², |√x-0|<ε. No negative-domain input is needed for endpoint continuity.

sessions.lesson:
Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT): a continuous real function on[a,b] takes every value between f(a) and f(b). In particular, opposite signs guarantee a zero in(a,b). We use this theorem with its hypotheses; its general real-analysis proof is not required here. It guarantees existence, not uniqueness. To establish uniqueness, one option is to prove f strictly increases: ifv>u thenf(v)>f(u).
Bisection maintains a closed bracket containing a root. Evaluate the midpoint; stop if it is a root, otherwise keep the half with opposite endpoint signs. After k halvings of initial widthW, width isW/2^k, and the current midpoint is at distance≤W/2^(k+1) from some bracketed root. The bound is non-strict unless the specification says otherwise.
Worked example: for f(x)=x²-2 on[1,2], signs are-1 and2. At3/2, f=1/4>0, so retain[1,3/2]. Its midpoint5/4 has error≤1/4 from the root. Uniqueness on positive inputs follows fromv²-u²=(v-u)(v+u)>0.
Guided practice: Starting with width6, what is the midpoint error bound after3 halvings? Check 6/16=3/8; do not confuse it with bracket width6/8.

sessions.lesson:
An absolute maximum is a value f(c) with f(c)≥f(x) for every domain x; it must be attained at a domain point c. A supremum is the least upper bound of the output set and need not be attained. The Extreme Value Theorem (EVT) guarantees both an attained maximum and minimum for a continuous real function on a closed bounded interval[a,b]. We use this theorem, not its full analysis proof. It guarantees existence, not where to look; elementary algebra can locate extrema in our examples.
Worked example: f(x)=2-(x-1)² on[-1,2]. Since0≤(x-1)²≤4, maximum2 occurs at1 and minimum-2 at-1. On the open interval(-1,2), the maximum2 remains, but the lower bound-2 is not attained, so there is no minimum.
Failure of a hypothesis means the theorem cannot guarantee the conclusion; it does not prove the conclusion false. A constant function on an open interval still attains its maximum and minimum.
Guided practice: f(x)=x on[0,3) has minimum0 and supremum3, but no maximum. The missing endpoint matters.

sessions.lesson:
A synthesis solution should identify the object, the approach and the requested guarantee before choosing a theorem. Is the variable an integer index or a real input? Is the target a finite value or a threshold beyond every bound? Which domain inputs are legal? A calculation of a candidate limit is only one part of a claim.
Worked audit: an approximation family F(h)=h²/(1+h²) tends to0 as h→0 because0≤F(h)≤h²; δ=√ε certifies error<ε. Sampling h=1/n creates a convergent sequence F(1/n), but sampled convergence alone would not prove a limit for an arbitrary function between samples. Here the uniform inequality does the work. DefiningF(0)=0 makes the formula continuous there. These are separate, connected conclusions.
Guided practice: For G(h)=|h|/(2+|h|), use G(h)≤|h|/2 to give both a function-limit certificate and one for G(1/n). Check δ=2ε, and any integerN>1/(2ε). Explain why a finite sample table would establish neither guarantee. In your independent work, choose your own legal transformation and bound; do not assume that the same denominator or error expression will recur.
